conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that whole-body vibration therapy is not proven to prevent fractures in people with osteoporosis and concludes with a definitive 'no' answer, stating that current evidence does not establish it as an effective fracture-prevention therapy.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
Whole-body vibration therapy is not proven to prevent fractures in people with osteoporosis. The available evidence base almost entirely addresses surrogate outcomes—bone mineral density (BMD), balance, and fall risk—rather than actual fracture incidence, which is the clinically meaningful endpoint.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of whole-body vibration (WBV) consistently report modest, inconsistent effects on BMD, particularly at the lumbar spine, but findings vary by protocol, population, and vibration platform, and many trials are small or methodologically weak (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12908257/; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13018-016-0357-2). A dedicated systematic review and meta-analysis explicitly investigating fracture risk in adults over 50 found data centered on fall rates and risk factors rather than confirmed reductions in actual fractures (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/50395745_The_Effect_of_8_Mos_of_Twice-Weekly_Low-_or_Higher_Intensity_Whole_Body_Vibration_on_Risk_Factors_for_Postmenopausal_Hip_Fracture).

Similarly, reviews on fall prevention—an important fracture risk factor—show mixed results across randomized controlled trials, with some studies noting improved balance but no clear evidence translating into significantly fewer falls or fractures (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02946-5).

Overall, no high-quality randomized controlled trial has directly demonstrated that WBV reduces fracture incidence in osteoporotic populations. Effects on BMD are inconsistent and generally small, and improvements in balance or muscle strength have not been convincingly linked to reduced fracture rates. This supports a "no" answer: while WBV may offer some ancillary benefits for bone health and neuromuscular function, current evidence does not establish it as an effective fracture-prevention therapy for osteoporosis.
